opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, and honestly I think the two are much more intertwined than people sometimes assume. There's a tendency to frame it as either "you need a bigger, better architecture" or "you need better data," but for editing in particular, what we've seen is that they unlock each other.

On the capability side, a strong base model gives you a lot for free. If the model already has a rich understanding of the visual world, how lighting works, how materials look, how objects relate to each other in a scene, then when you ask it to change one thing, it has the knowledge it needs to make that change look plausible. Editing is in some ways harder than generation, because you're not just producing a nice image, you're producing a nice image that has to agree with an existing one in all the places you didn't ask to change. That requires the model to really understand what's in the input, not just what's in the prompt. So things like how the model encodes the source image, how much it can attend to fine detail, and whether it can reason about identity and structure, all of that matters a lot for consistency.

But data is where I think a lot of the real progress on fidelity has come from. The challenge with editing is that naturally occurring paired data, the same scene before and after one specific change, is really rare. You don't find millions of photos on the internet where someone changed only the color of a jacket and nothing else. So a lot of the work is in constructing that data: synthesizing pairs, using video frames where things change naturally over time, using existing models to generate candidates and then filtering very aggressively for quality. And the filtering part is underrated. If your training pairs have subtle drift, a face shifting slightly, background texture changing, the model learns that drift is acceptable, and you see it in the outputs. Clean, carefully curated pairs teach the model that preservation is part of the task.

So the way I'd put it is: capability sets the ceiling for what kinds of edits are possible at all, and data determines how reliably and precisely you hit that ceiling. And they feed back into each other, because better models let you generate better synthetic data, which trains better models. That loop has been one of the most productive things in the field over the last couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says model capability and data are “intertwined” and “unlock each other,” describing them as jointly driving editing quality.

r002.rationale: The response says capability sets the ceiling while data determines reliability and precision. It does not clearly attribute proficiency at specific editing tasks primarily to training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that they're inseparable, but they fail in different ways, and that's what tells you where to put your effort.

Model capability is really about the prior. A good base model already "knows" what a plausible image looks like: how light falls, how a face holds together when you turn it, what a reflection should do when you move an object. That prior is what gives you fidelity. When you ask for an edit and the result looks photographic rather than pasted on, that's the model's understanding of the world doing the work. You can't get that from edit data alone, because no edit dataset is going to cover every material, every lighting condition, every pose.

Training data is about the mapping. The model might know what a plausible image is, but it doesn't inherently know what "make it look like golden hour but keep everything else" means, or that "change the shirt" should not touch the hands. That's where paired data comes in. And consistency, which I'd argue is the harder of the two, is almost entirely a data problem. The model has to learn that the identity of this person, the texture of that wall, the exact crop, are things it's supposed to preserve by default. Left to its own devices, a generative model would rather regenerate than preserve, because regeneration is what it was pretrained to do. You have to actively teach restraint, and you teach it with examples.

The tricky part is that good paired edit data is hard to get. Real before-and-after pairs are scarce, and synthetic pairs inherit the biases of whatever produced them. So in practice a lot of the craft is bootstrapping: using the model's own prior to generate candidates, filtering aggressively, and feeding back the ones that actually preserved what they should. Capability improves the data you can make, and that data improves capability. It's a loop, not a trade-off.

If you forced me to pick, I'd say the base model sets the ceiling on fidelity, and the data determines whether you ever reach it on the specific edit someone actually asked for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says model capability and training data are inseparable and describes them as improving each other in a loop.

r002.rationale: It says training data teaches the mapping from specific edit instructions to changes, including examples such as changing a shirt without altering hands.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re deeply connected. The model needs enough capacity to understand the image and the instruction, but also to preserve everything the instruction doesn’t ask it to change. That’s a different challenge from generating a compelling image from scratch. You can produce a beautiful result and still fail at editing because you changed the person’s identity or altered the background.

The training data has to teach that distinction. Ideally, you have examples where the input and output are closely aligned, and the requested edit explains the difference between them. If those examples contain unrelated changes, the model gets a noisy signal about what it’s supposed to preserve.

So I wouldn’t frame it as capabilities versus data. Better capabilities let the model learn more complex transformations, while better data makes those transformations precise and controllable. And when we evaluate the result, we need to look at both sides: did it make the requested change, and did it keep everything else consistent?

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities and training data are “deeply connected” and describes how both contribute to precise, controllable edits.

r002.rationale: The response gives training data an important role, but does not say proficiency at specific editing tasks comes primarily from training data; it presents capabilities and data as complementary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they go hand in hand. The model needs the capacity to understand both the image and the instruction, but the training data has to teach it what a good edit actually looks like. That means making the requested change while preserving everything that should stay the same.

That preservation part is really important. If you ask to change someone’s shirt, you don’t want their face or the background to change as well. So having examples where the input and output are consistent, except for the intended edit, gives the model a much clearer learning signal.

A more capable model can help with understanding complex instructions and generating realistic details. But if the data doesn’t demonstrate that consistency, increasing model capacity alone doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. You need both the ability to make the change and the supervision to learn when to leave things alone.

r001.rationale: The response says model ability and training data “go hand in hand,” with capability enabling edits and data teaching what a good, consistent edit looks like.

r002.rationale: The response gives training data an important teaching role, but does not say that training data is the primary source of proficiency at specific editing tasks; it describes capability and data as jointly necessary.
